title.en: The Sliding Window: Turn O(n²) Into O(n)

description.en: Recomputing a sum for every window is wasteful. Slide the window instead — add the new element, drop the old — and a quadratic loop becomes linear. The interview pattern you'll use forever.

story_variants.en:
## Stop Recomputing What You Already Know

"You want the highest total of any 3 consecutive days of sales," Vaathiyaar says. "The naive way re-adds three numbers for every position — O(n·k) work. But when the window slides one step right, you already know the old sum. Just **add the entering value and subtract the leaving one**. One addition, one subtraction, per step. That's the **sliding window**."

### The Move

Keep a running `window_sum`. To slide from position `i-k` to `i`:

> window_sum += arr[i] − arr[i − k]

The element entering on the right is added; the one falling off the left is subtracted. The window's size stays fixed; only its edges move. Track the best sum as you go.

```
[2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]  window size 3
first window 2+1+5 = 8
slide: +1 -2 -> 7 ... +3 -1 -> 9 ... +2 -5 -> 6
best = 9
```

This turns an O(n·k) scan into a single O(n) pass — the difference between instant and sluggish on large inputs. The same pattern powers "longest substring", "max average", rate limiters, and moving averages.

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** if you're recomputing an overlapping range, slide instead of restart. The overlap is free information — use it.

Today you implement `max_window_sum(arr, k)` — the largest sum of any `k` consecutive elements.

explanation.en: Compute the first window's sum once
It's the best we've seen so far
Slide the window one step at a time
Add the entering value, subtract the leaving value

instruction.en: Implement `max_window_sum(arr, k)` — the largest sum of any `k` consecutive elements, using the sliding-window trick (compute the first window once, then slide by adding the entering element and subtracting the leaving one). Then print `max_window_sum([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], 3)` (expected: `9`).

def max_window_sum(arr: list, k: int) -> int:
    """Largest sum of any k consecutive elements (sliding window)."""
    window = sum(arr[:k])
    best = window
    # slide: for i in range(k, len(arr)): window += arr[i] - arr[i-k]; update best
    pass

print(max_window_sum([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], 3))

en: Start with window = sum(arr[:k]) and best = window
Slide: for i in range(k, len(arr)): window += arr[i] - arr[i-k]
After each slide, update best if window is larger

q.en: When a window of size k slides one step right to end at index i, how should window_sum change?

en: Subtract arr[i] and add arr[i - k]
Add arr[i] only; the window grows by one

q.en: Max sum of any k consecutive elements: naive re-adding costs O(n·k). What does the sliding window cost?
q.ta: தொடர்ச்சியான k உறுப்புகளின் அதிகபட்ச கூட்டுத்தொகை: naive முறை O(n·k). sliding window-இன் செலவு என்ன?

en: O(n·k), the same as the naive way
O(k), only the window size matters
O(n²), since every window is visited

q.en: Bug hunt: in the slide loop someone wrote window += arr[i] - arr[i-1]. What is wrong?
q.ta: பிழையைக் கண்டுபிடி: slide loop-இல் ஒருவர் window += arr[i] - arr[i-1] என்று எழுதினார். என்ன தவறு?

en: It drops the wrong element; the leaving one is arr[i - k]
Subtracting is unsafe; recompute with sum() instead
It should be arr[i+1] - arr[i] to look ahead
Nothing; arr[i-1] is the element leaving the window
ta: தவறான உறுப்பைக் கழிக்கிறது; வெளியேறுவது arr[i - k]
கழிப்பது பாதுகாப்பற்றது; sum() மூலம் மீண்டும் கணக்கிடு
முன்னோக்கிப் பார்க்க arr[i+1] - arr[i] என்று இருக்க வேண்டும்
எதுவும் இல்லை; window-இலிருந்து வெளியேறுவது arr[i-1] தான்

uth_example:
temps = [31, 33, 35, 30, 28, 34, 36, 37]
k = 3

window = sum(temps[:k])
moving_avg = [round(window / k, 1)]
for i in range(k, len(temps)):
    window += temps[i] - temps[i - k]     # add the new day, drop the oldest
    moving_avg.append(round(window / k, 1))

hottest = max(range(len(moving_avg)), key=lambda i: moving_avg[i])
print("3-day averages:", moving_avg)
print("hottest stretch:", temps[hottest:hottest + k])
